Daily briefing: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that by harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV.
  • Industry observers note that the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine.
  • Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

It has been revealed that by harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV. This year, several research teams described vaccination strategies that triggered the production of these broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in monkeys, and precursors to bnAbs in people, suggesting that an effective vaccine is possible. But devastating cuts to US funding for HIV research have left some efforts in limbo.

Industry observers note that the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine. It also has a drug capable of preventing infections: the long-acting injectable drug lenacapavir, which could avert an estimated one-third of new HIV infections in Africa if given to just 5% of adults. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back, argues a Nature editorial.

Reference: UNAIDS & Gates Foundation report.

Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people. Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented last week at the US Society for Neuroscience annual meeting, could help to explain maternal mental-health conditions such as postpartum depression.

In a recent development, ‘General purpose’ artificial-intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are impressing researchers with their emerging biology skills, including protein design and structure prediction. In some tests, these models have even outperformed those designed specifically for biology tasks and trained on vast troves of protein-sequence data. Some scientists predict that generalist AI tools could eventually catch up with, or surpass, blockbuster models such as AlphaFold. Others suggest these latest abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data, rather than advanced learning.

As I write, the United States army is preparing to detonate around 4.4 tonnes of unstable lead azide, a chemical used to make munitions, at an ammunition plant in Iowa. “It's essentially a lead bomb,” indicates occupational and environmental health researcher Patrick O’Shaughnessy. “Now it's a matter of how much gets ejected out of the bunker.” Academic researchers have banded together to gather independent public data about the plume of toxic lead dust that is expected to spread over the area.

Figure 1 | Position verification. a, To check the location of a party called the prover, two verifiers each send a random bit (a challenge), which are timed to reach the location simultaneously. The prover combines the bits and returns the answer. Because no signal travels faster than light, a prompt reply shows that the prover is at the location. b, However, if two adversaries, one near each verifier, copy a challenge and pass it to each other, they can answer in time even though nobody is at the claimed location. c, In Kavuri and colleagues’ scheme, one verifier generates two entangled photons, keeping one and sending the other to the prover. Both verifiers then transmit classical challenges. The prover uses the challenges to determine how to measure its photon and returns the result, while the first verifier measures the other photon. If the prover’s result arrives in time and the two measurements pass a statistical check (a Bell test), the transmitted photon must have been measured at the claimed location.

Industry observers note that “Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake,” notes physicist Davide Bacco. Now researchers have outlined an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using quantum entanglement.

In a, two verifiers send random bits (challenges) timed to reach the claimed location simultaneously. The prover combines them and replies. Because signals cannot travel faster than light, a prompt response verifies the prover’s location. But two adversaries (b) can defeat this test by exchanging the challenges and responding in time. In (c), a verifier also sends one of two entangled photons, which are inexorably linked in a way that can be proven using a statistical check (a Bell test). If the prover’s result arrives inside the time window imposed by the speed of light and the photons pass the Bell test, the prover must be inside the target region. (Nature | 9 min read).

According to recent reports, chemist George Whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields, including patterning surfaces with molecules — a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices — advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.” In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to”, notes polymer scientist Joseph DeSimone. “In fact, he made it exciting not to.” Whitesides has died, aged 87.

Read Whitesides’s guide to writing a scientific paper in a special problem of Advanced Materials that celebrated his 65th birthday.

Some mental disorders seem to take different forms in different places, writes mental-illness researcher Alexander Pereira. “Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears,” he writes — with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, prevalent in China, and psychological symptoms, such as low self-esteem, more common in the West. Pereira argues that our ability to adapt to our social environment might significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental health.

In a recent development, changing location — even just walking through a doorway — can signal to our brains that work is over and it’s time to relax, states cognitive scientist Joan Ongchoco. (BBC Future | 11 min read).

Reference: Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology paper.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03879-2.

Today I’m impressed and amazed by entrepreneur Georgia Waddington, who represented New Zealand in the Miss Universe pageant wearing an 18 kg dress representing the Pink Terraces of Lake Rotomahana. The stunning geological formation was buried in the 1886 eruption of Mt Tarawera, but it will never be forgotten.

It has been revealed that while I blueprint a recreation of the Zanclean megaflood tonight in the bath, why not send me your feedback on this newsletter? Your e-mails are always welcome at briefing@nature.com.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months.

Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time. In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported.

These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips, and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another glitch: tightened security against the distillation of AI models.

Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information, this is an concern that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months.

If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google, and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks.

In a recent development, it's important to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains.

With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them?

Recent findings suggest that china still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with owners, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months.

Sources indicate that with devices like the RTX Spark, AMD's AI Halo, and more, people are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap.

This is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official.

Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts presently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s.

Sources indicate that if China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.

#773. Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (932 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Nature)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.
  • Open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere.
  • An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.

Open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere. Industries that rely heavily on scientific discoveries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, disproportionately cite open-access work in their patents over paywalled research, a study has found.

An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.

Industry observers note that when the study authors expanded the definition of open access to include papers available on Sci-Hub, a website that hosts pirated copies of scientific articles, this over-representation was even stronger. Papers that were freely available (either through the journal publishers or Sci-Hub) were 3.41 times more prevalent in patent citations than they were in the wider scientific literature.

The findings, published in Scientometrics, show how heavily inventors lean on open-access research, indicates study co-author Abdelghani Maddi, a scientometrics researcher at Sorbonne University in Paris. When you include platforms such as Sci-Hub, “the numbers are striking”, he says. “Open science is not only about who can read science, it’s about who can build on it.”.

Industry observers note that for their analysis, Maddi and his colleagues leveraged the ‘Reliance on Science’ data set, a publicly available tool that identifies citation links between patents and journal publications2. They found that research-intensive industries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, cite the scientific literature (both open and pay-walled) in their patents much more heavily than do more engineering-based industries, such as vehicle- and construction-equipment manufacturing.

The researchers also demonstrated that patents from countries with a high proportion of high-tech industries, including South Korea, Singapore and Denmark, cite more scientific publications than do those from countries with more heavy manufacturing industries, such as South Africa, Brazil and Italy.

It has been revealed that to track patent citations of open-access papers specifically, the team cross-referenced research publications in the Reliance on Science patent database against those in OpenAlex, an index that catalogues hundreds of millions of scientific documents. They then used a normalization metric to account for differences in open-access publishing practices across research disciplines. Open-access publishing is much more prevalent in the health sciences than it is in computer science, for example, says Maddi.

Seeing how open-access papers were over-represented in patent citations suggests that making research freely accessible does more than just help people to read and share scientific findings, notes study co-author Francesco De Pretis, an applied mathematician at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia in Italy. It also makes that knowledge more likely to be used in developing fresh technologies and inventions, he adds. “Our findings show that open science is not just a matter for academia, it’s also the business of industry and of national economies.”.

In a recent development, matt Marx, an innovation and entrepreneurship researcher at Cornell University in Ithaca, Latest York, whose team developed the Reliance on Science database, says the finding that patents tend to cite open-access papers “is especially intriguing”. But he cautions against assuming that ease of access is the only factor at play. “Perhaps inventors are more likely to cite papers they can read because those are open access, or it could be that prominent or key papers are more likely to be open-source,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of the exact causes, the access barrier is real, claims Marin Dacos, who heads the open-science taskforce in France’s Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space. Negotiating contracts with thousands of journal publishers worldwide requires specialist library staff — a resource that is generally only available to large companies and universities, he says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've bought the big stuff: the SSDs, the RAM, the graphics card. Those are the obvious Black Friday deals for a PC gamer, but this is the perfect opportunity to step back and look at the gadgets and tools that you wouldn't normally think about, or even know about. That's where this SinLoon external power button comes in, on sale for just $11.19.

According to recent reports, we'd normally run through all of the significant, vital specs here, but we don't really need to do that here because, well, there isn't any. You're buying an external power button. It connects to your PC. It turns it off, it turns it on, it restarts it (if you want it to). It has a two-meter cable that you can use to connect it to your PC, either using your PC's front panel with the supplied splitter or directly to your motherboard. It's also, by design, got a pair of mechanical keyboard keys: these'll be the ones you press to turn your rig on or off.

● Check out this deal at Amazon.

According to recent reports, this gaming-friendly external power button has a 2-meter (78.74 inch) cable, along with a splitter that lets you connect both buttons to your case's front panel buttons. It also includes adhesive pads and zip-ties.

Industry observers note that simple enough, then, but that's not to downplay what you're getting here, or how it's been made. Mechanical keyboard keys are an interesting choice, because they look like they've been plucked straight from a top-spec gaming keyboard, especially with the RGB lighting underneath. It's a showstopper by design. SinLoon could have just gone for a significant, round button, but by going for a design that uses mechanical keyboard keys, they're making sure this button has longevity.

Industry observers note that that's why SinLoon reckons these keys are good for no less than five million keystrokes. You can switch your PC on or off five million times before this board wears out. That's a lot of restarts. The two keys themselves sit in a smooth, black plastic case. The wiring is black, too, and sheathed (mostly) in glossy plastic, extending from the back. It does eventually split into different colored cables, though, each labeled so you know their purpose and where you'll need to connect them.

While you will need to open up your PC to get this installed, it's an easy enough process, as long as your case lets you get close to your PC's front panel headers. PC builders won't have much trouble with this, as you've probably already dealt with these cables when you've hooked it up to your motherboard. It's the same process for these cables, and it comes with connectors to handle the power and disk access LEDs, too.

Recent findings suggest that you don't have to sacrifice your PC's power buttons, either. This SinLoon power button comes with a 1-to-2 splitter, a physical adapter that lets you connect these cables alongside the cables handling your PC's power and reset buttons. It's a physical adapter, so if the pinout doesn't quite match up, you can just move the header cables around until it works. You can also totally bypass your PC's power button, if you prefer, by just connecting the cables up to your motherboard without the splitter.

You may not need this, but for $11, it's the ultimate buy for a techie's desk. You might not have ever thought about a desktop power button, but look: it's cool, and it's useful. It's not just a pointless desk ornament, but a practical tool that'll help you turn your rig on or off. If you've got your PC in a place that's difficult to reach, it solves an obvious problem, too.

You'll also find it useful if you're a maker or builder. For instance, open test rigs (like the ones we use at Tom's Hardware) might not have a case, just a motherboard on a desk with a bunch of parts attached. Rather than shorting the header pins to start your rig (not the best idea), you can attach this SinLoon button instead to make the whole process safer and easier.

The $11.19 sale price for this SinLoon external power button is cheap enough to make it easy to justify. It'll rapidly improve a quality-of-life issue at your desk and it'll look cool doing it, especially if you've already got RGB peripherals on your desk to match. Whether it's for yourself or as a gift for a PC builder in your life, grab this cool desk item on sale while the discount lasts.

There's more to gaming than having the latest $7,000 GPU. Black Friday is a great time to pick up some new gaming peripherals, which will significantly improve your gaming experience at a fraction of the cost of, well, $7,000.

Some of our favorite gaming mice are currently on sale — both the current generation and the last generation, and, let's face it: a lot of last-gen gaming mice are very, very similar to the current generation. So now is the time to pick up a gaming mouse or two, as there's almost certainly something on sale that will work for you, whether you're looking for an ultra-lightweight, stripped-down mouse for competitive eSports, or a multi-functional, multi-button mouse for MMOs (and some productivity on the side).

Sources indicate that if the allure of the DeathAdder V4 Pro's upgraded sensor and significantly improved battery life are calling your name, great news — this mouse is also currently on sale for just $137.74 at Amazon — or $129.99, if you don't mind the Niko-branded version. The DeathAdder V4 Pro features Razer's Focus Pro 45K Gen-2 optical sensor, which has a maximum resolution of 45,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 900 IPS, and can handle up to 85G's of force. It weighs just 56g and has the same shape and size as its predecessor.

Sources indicate that this mouse sports Razer's Focus Pro 45K Gen-2 sensor and gets up to 150 hours of battery life. It comes with an 8,000 Hz polling dongle and features a silver, black, and white pattern associated with esports competitor NiKo, but the regular versions of the mouse are also on sale.

The DeathAdder V4 Pro features Razer's Gen-4 optical switches, which are rated for 100 million clicks and feel and sound different than the switches in the DeathAdder V3 Pro — they're lighter and have a slightly higher, more hollow-sounding click, but they feel great. The notched optical scroll wheel also feels lighter, and I found it felt more accurate and precise than the DeathAdder V3 Pro's scroll wheel despite having freer movement.

Read our full review of the DeathAdder V4 Pro here.

The Basilisk V3 Pro is basically the last generation of the Basilisk lineup. The Basilisk V3 Pro isn't as performance-focused as is the DeathAdder V3 Pro — this ergonomically-contoured wireless gaming mouse also features Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 30,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 70G's of force. It has 11 programmable buttons and 13 zones of bright, customizable RGB lighting, and it weighs 3.95 ounces (112g).

Razer's flagship wireless Basilisk V3 Pro features Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, Gen-3 optical mouse switches, and 13 zones of bright RGB underglow lighting. It gets up to 110 hours of battery life and is compatible with Razer's HyperPolling Wireless Dongle and Mouse Dock Pro.

Like the DeathAdder V3 Pro, this mouse also works with Razer's HyperPolling Wireless Dongle (sold separately) to get up to an 8,000 Hz wireless polling rate; it's also compatible with Razer's Mouse Dock Pro (sold separately), which integrates the HyperPolling Wireless Dongle and also allows for wireless charging (and also features 8 zones of customizable RGB lighting, because why not).

Read our full review of the Basilisk V3 Pro here.

It has been revealed that if you're looking for something ultra-light, well, it's in the name: the Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 is a pseudo-ambidextrous ultra-lightweight mouse weighing just 2.12 ounces (60g) and designed for those who need speed above all else. And it's currently on sale at Logitech's website for $74.99 — nearly 60% off its retail price of $179.99.

Logitech's ultralight 60g wireless mouse features a pseudo-ambidextrous symmetrical shape and sports the brand's Hero 2 optical sensor and Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches.

Recent findings suggest that the Pro X Superlight 2 features Logitech's Hero 2 optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 32,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 500 IPS, and can handle up to 40G's of force. It has five programmable buttons; its primary buttons feature Logitech's Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches, which can actuate both optically (for the lowest latency) and mechanically (for saving power).

Read our full review of the Pro X Superlight 2 here.

It has been revealed that logitech's G502 X Plus is still one of our favorite mice — both for its comfortable, ergonomic right-handed shape and its pretty, bright RGB light strip. Not to mention its comfortable button layout and top-of-the-line sensor, which has been improved through a firmware update to Logitech's Hero 44K, with a maximum resolution of 44,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 678 IPS, and up to 40 G's of acceleration.

This versatile, ergonomic gaming mouse features Logitech's Hero 44K optical sensor and gets up to 130 hours of battery life with the lighting turned off.

Sources indicate that the G502 X Plus has 13 programmable controls and features a handful of extra buttons — an adjustable DPI shift / trigger button, as well as two button on the side of the left mouse button. It comes with a dual-mode tilt wheel that switches between frictionless free-spin and precise, notched scrolling at the click of a switch, and feels great. It also comes in four colors now, including the recently-introduced black/purple and white/mint colorways, and all four colors are currently on sale.

Read our full Logitech G502 X Plus review here.

Maybe ultralight and stripped-down gaming mice aren't your thing. If you're looking for a mouse with all the buttons, Corsair's Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is a good option, and it's presently on sale for almost 50% off at Best Buy — you can pick it up for just $69.99, which is 46% off its original MSRP of $139.99.

Sources indicate that this MMO / MOBA-focused mouse features 16 programmable buttons, 12 of which are on its customizable, movable side panel. It also sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force.

The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless features 16 programmable buttons, 12 of which are on its movable side panel — you can move the side panel forward or backward, depending on your hand size and what's most comfortable for you. It sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force. It weighs 4.02 ounces (114g), but let's face it — if you're looking for a mouse with 16 programmable buttons, weight is not your top priority. The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless also features a pretty solid battery life of 150 hours over its 2.4GHz wireless connection, which means you'll only have to charge it every couple of weeks (and that's if you're a serious gamer).

Read our full review of the Scimitar Elite SE Wireless here.

If you're looking for something modular and potentially customizable, HyperX's Pulsefire Saga Pro is a wireless gaming mouse with a couple of modular options in the box, plus the ability to print your own pieces. This lightweight gaming mouse also features five programmable buttons and up to a 4,000 Hz wireless polling rate, and it's right now on sale at Best Buy for $79.99 — $40 off its MSRP of $119.99.

Recent findings suggest that this ultra-lightweight wireless mouse is modular and comes with 2 humps, 2 sets of primary buttons, and 2 sets of side buttons. It features up to a 4,000 Hz wireless polling rate and HyperX's 26K sensor.

It has been revealed that the Pulsefire Saga Pro sports HyperX's 26K sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 26,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 650 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force. This is the same sensor we've seen in HyperX's mice for a couple of years now — it's a solid sensor in terms of speed and accuracy, but it might not be for you if you're looking for the latest and greatest.

However, if you're just looking for lightweight modularity, the Pulsefire Saga Pro is where it's at: this mouse comes with two mouse humps, two sets of primary mouse buttons, and two sets of side buttons, and it implements its modularity well — everything fits together nicely and feels sturdy, and we had no complications with creaking or parts moving around in our testing. All configurations will give you a weight of 2.54 ounces (72g).

Real deals on gaming graphics cards are few and far between this Black Friday, but PowerColor's Reaper RX 9070 GRE is a standout. In a gaming GPU market that's starving for midrange options after prices on affordable 16GB graphics cards went to the moon, this $619 9070 GRE gives you a massive step up over cards like the RTX 5060 Ti and RX 9060 XT for way less than those ostensibly entry-midrange cards are selling for today.

Recent findings suggest that I use PowerColor's Reaper RX 9070 and RX 9070 XT in the Tom's Hardware labs as the representative samples of those cards for our GPU Hierarchy testing, and this RX 9070 GRE uses a similar cooler design. They're cool and quiet, and their slim two-slot heatsinks with full-length metal backplates will fit into even SFF systems with ease. You don't get any RGB LED flair, but many will consider that an advantage nowadays.

In other words, these cards give you everything you need and nothing you don't.

The Radeon RX 9070 GRE offers great 1080p and 1440p gaming performance for a low price in today's crazy market, and it gives you access to AMD's high-quality FSR 4 upscaler for a performance boost when you need it.

According to recent reports, in our 2026 GPU Hierarchy testing, the RX 9070 GRE delivers a solid 90 FPS average across all our raster and RT testing at 1080p and clears the 60 FPS average bar for 1440p. That's impressive performance for a relatively inexpensive card today.

It has been revealed that if you favor raster gaming, the 9070 GRE looks even better. It can churn out a high-refresh-rate-ready 120 FPS at 1080p and 90 FPS at 1440p. And all that is before you add in high-quality FSR 4 upscaling, which boosts performance and looks better than most games' native TAA implementations.

Between its compact, quiet cooler, strong performance, and low price, this PowerColor card is a real GPU deal this Black Friday, and if you need a real bang-for-the-buck upgrade in a graphics card market that's increasingly hostile to gamers, this may be your last chance at a real value upgrade. Get one while you can.

#765. China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Tomshardware)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S.
  • More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion intends in the first half of 2026.
  • It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require.

More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion intends in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is crucial because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials.

It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.

Industry observers note that PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities, the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process.

Industry observers note that as well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. Fresh grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. The increasingly common use of harder laminates is resulting in the bits being consumed more quickly.

That’s good news for those making drill bits: HSBC forecasts global demand growing 55% a year in the coming three years. And as with many parts of the AI revolution, the voracious appetite of the sector means that supplies can’t keep up. Even with manufacturers increasing production, the bank forecasts a 24% supply shortfall in PCB drill bits in 2027.

In a recent development, that could push the world towards Chinese suppliers, right as the west is trying to wean itself off a dependency on the country for rare earths and other elements necessary to make GPUs. Guangdong Dtech, based in China, is the world’s largest PCB drill bit maker by volume. Around three in every 10 drill bits made in 2025 come from the firm, with its monthly capacity potentially climbing from 160 million bits in June to more than 235 million by year-end. Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers are still dominant at the premium end of the market, according to consultancy Frost & Sullivan, though Chinese manufacturers are trying to close that gap.

In its 2026 interim results, Dtech reported that it had begun mass-producing drill bits with aspect ratios exceeding 40:1, while developing techniques for producing bits exceeding 60:1. Its newer diamond-coated tools for particularly tough M9+ board materials have also entered small-scale use.

Sources indicate that it’s not just in drill bits that China has a chokehold. Another Chinese manufacturer, Defu Technology, has historically been a key supplier of copper foil for lithium-ion batteries, but is increasingly changing its manufacturing processes to try and capitalise on the AI boom. “AI server PCB/CCL upgrades require smoother HVLP copper foil to reduce high-speed signal loss,” writes Avery Chan, a JP Morgan analyst.

HVLP stands for hyper-very-low-profile copper foil, and its manufacturers must make the surface smooth enough to minimise signal loss while making sure it can still stick to the insulating material it is attached to.

The business has historically been dominated by suppliers outside mainland China, with Japan’s Mitsui Kinzoku and Furukawa Electric, and Taiwan’s Co-Tech, holding more than 60% of global HVLP supply in 2025. Defu is trying to break in to disrupt that, with the firm shipping around 700 tonnes of HVLP foil in September, including more than 180 tonnes of HVLP4. JP Morgan’s Chan forecasts a shortage of qualified HVLP4 supply of around 700 tonnes a month in 2026, rising to 1,200 tonnes in 2027. Defu aims to add 50,000 tonnes of annual high-end PCB foil capacity over 2027 and 2028. But all the foil it creates will have to get past stringent testing.

Even before finished chips reach a server, they must be tested using specialist probe cards and sockets, which themselves rely on sophisticated PCBs of a type not found in a server but just used to check whether the chips work. “PCB is becoming the bottleneck and the value-add in probe cards,” wrote JP Morgan analyst Jerry Tsai.

Because of that, China is focusing attention there, too. In September, its Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and National Development and Reform Commission published a five-year plan calling for advances in high-frequency, high-speed and densely layered PCBs, alongside copper-clad laminates, low-profile copper foil and specialist manufacturing equipment.

But China won’t see the benefits of building newly introduced factories immediately. Producing the most sophisticated PCBs requires experience, specialist equipment and the ability to manufacture complex designs consistently at scale. Tsai warned that “the learning curve is measured in years, rather than quarters.”.

A throwback to the golden age of mascot-driven platformers, Waltz and Jam looks like a revival of a classic series that doesn’t actually exist. You’ll play as a ghost and its dog as they journey through the afterlife. With levels inspired by the seven deadly sins, Waltz and Jam looks to breathe some delightfully creative ideas into one of gaming’s foundational genres.

Co-op enthusiasts are getting a cozy little treat this December with Hela: Of Mice and Magic. Inspired by the sights of Northern Sweden, you and your friends will play as tiny mice exploring a big world. The pastoral adventure might be the perfect destressor after a few weeks of crime sprees.

Industry observers note that the survival crafting genre is about to get much smaller. Trollheim: Gnomes is a co-op game that lets up to eight players control gnomes looking for shelter in a vast forest. Inspired by Nordic folklore, the early access game looks to capture some of the same magic that has made Valheim a smash hit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games is justifiably proud of everything it put into Grand Theft Auto 6, and one technical detail the studio has taken the time to highlight is the game's vehicle physics simulation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games is justifiably proud of everything it put into Grand Theft Auto 6, and one technical detail the studio has taken the time to highlight is the game's vehicle physics simulation. According to Ben Lyons, Rockstar's technical director for physics, some of the team started building and racing cars after finishing Grand Theft Auto 5, even winning in their class at the Nürbrugring 24 hours.

"This taught us a huge amount about how to modify, design, and set up real cars to go fast and what happens to them when things go wrong, like bursting tires and crashing," Lyons told Polygon in a statement. (As if to underline the point, Lyons' LinkedIn profile pic highlights him proudly holding up a blown racecar tire in a pit garage.) "We also took the same approach with rally-racing dirt bikes — it’s important to us to understand the difference between racing on two and four wheels and on- versus off-road so we can give our players as convincing authentic experience as we can," he stated. "For this game, we completely rewrote the vehicle simulation for every vehicle type so we could add more detail and realism, as well as authenticity and believability, to the game.".

Knowing how detail-obsessed Rockstar's developers are, and how seemingly limitless their resources were, I wondered if GTA 6's handling physics would be able to hold their own against the best the racing game genre has to offer​​​​​​​. My interest was doubly piqued when Polygon's reviewer Giovanni Colantonio told me there was a ton of racing in the game, both in the form of organized events on racing circuits and impromptu street races. Could GTA 6 secretly be a great racing game, along with everything else?

The answer is: no, not really. The cars are great to drive, and the races can be fun, but the design and technology of GTA 6 are fundamentally not set up for racing, and it shows.

Recent findings suggest that as a benchmark to measure GTA 6 against, I chose Forza Horizon 6. It wouldn't be right to compare Rockstar's everything-game to the most realistic circuit-racing sims, but an open-world racing game that has entertaining, accessible, and credible driving physics, with a degree of depth, seemed like fair game.

Sources indicate that GTA 6's racing options are hardly minor. Street-racing leagues unlock in chapter 3, but you can roll up to any circuit and start racing, or log some time trial laps, from the very beginning. A racing career is even a viable way to make money in the game. If you have enough cash for the entry fee and to rent a competitive ride (or you could just steal one), the payouts for top-three placements represent a decent profit.

It has been revealed that as a driving — as opposed to racing — game, there are a number of things that GTA 6 actually does better than Forza. For starters, there's the clearest fruit of Lyons' racing experience: the damage modelling. It's not as astounding as the soft-body physics in BeamNG.drive, but GTA 6 does have extremely detailed and reactive damage that meaningfully affects car handling and performance as well as smashing and peeling away body panels. Big plus.

In a recent development, I've already written about GTA 6's genius use of the PS5 DualSense controllers' adaptive triggers to allow for easy, relaxed driving at cruising speeds when exploring or just driving from place to place. That's something I wish Forza Horizon could have. And while Forza Horizon 6's Japan has more outright beautiful scenery than GTA 6's Leonida, the incredible richness and detail of Rockstar's game makes it an equal or greater pleasure to explore. The roads are much busier with traffic, all of which seems to be driven by reactive (if somewhat chaotic) humans rather than Forza's silent automatons. Also — not an insignificant detail when it comes to the cruising experience — the radio stations are much better.

Sources indicate that for sheer driving pleasure, I wouldn't put GTA 6 ahead of Forza, but it's not far behind. The rolling gait of its soft-suspension civilian rides makes them fun (if not easy) to chuck around, and drifts and tail-wagging burnouts are easy and satisfying to pull off. You get a good sense of the surface you're driving on when off-roading, and the world around you has much more credible and reactive physics than it does in Forza, including things like mud and street furniture (which, in Forza, all appears to be made from either balsa wood or the hardest substance known to man).

In a recent development, but anywhere where you care to examine the games' racing chops, Forza wins out. GTA 6's car customization has great cosmetic options, but the performance upgrades are rudimentary compared to Forza's. Forza has a manual transmission option, which, if you want to use it, grants much finer control over, and connection with, the car.

When you're actually racing, the gulf opens up. GTA's racing AI is in the spirit of the whole game's AI: it's chaotic, violent, and random. Races are tough to win because anything can happen, not because the racers are actually competitive. They're knockabout, almost slapstick affairs in which there's seldom any sign of anyone trying to follow a racing line. I've been in GTA 6 races with five or six cars driving abreast down the straight and then sideswiping each other on the corners. It's madness.

In the end, GTA 6's most profound failing as a racing game might also be its subtlest. It's the camera. It's not just that there's no in-car or first-person view (unless you're looking at your phone, which I do not recommend). Even the chase cameras, which look much like those of Forza Horizon 6, are just not as well tuned for racing. I'm not quite sure why — I think it has something to do with elevation and field of view, as well as the way the camera moves with the car as it turns — but it's much harder to pick and hold a line through a corner in GTA 6. You feel as though you're pushing your car around the circuit from above rather than sitting in it.

This effect isn't helped by the undefined track design, the handling model's tendency toward understeer, and the lack of audio and tactile feedback about where the edge of the car's grip is. Specifically when racing, GTA 6 feels woolly, where Forza is razor sharp.

This is a fundamentally unfair exercise; GTA 6 isn't a racing game, and it isn't really trying to be. As a driving game, it's hugely pleasurable, with a distinctive character and an amazing world to explore. The races are a fun diversion. But if you compare them to a true racer like Forza Horizon 6, you get a very swift and clear lesson in design intention. It doesn't matter how much money or detail went into GTA 6, or how good its physics model is; compared to something that was built for purpose, it ends up looking sloppy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Original Article was published on 14 October 2026.

Correction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11162-7Published online 14 October 2026.

Sources indicate that in the version of the article initially published, in Table 1, the number of BAT– patients with BMI < 25 was “8,826” but should have been “8,626”. In Fig. 2f, “β = 0.077” should have read “β = –0.077”. In the Fig. 2c legend, “(n = 2,680 per tertile)” should have read “(n = 2,903 per tertile)”. In Extended Data Fig. 1c and e, the minus sign was missing from both correlation coefficients and has now been added. In the caption for Fig. j–l, “losartan-treated mice (n = 7) and controls (n = 5)” should have been “losartan-treated mice (n = 5) and controls (n = 7)”. In the Extended Data Fig. 9 legend, “All p values except (g) obtained using unpaired, two tailed t-test” should have been “All p values except (b,g) obtained using unpaired, two tailed t-test”; in the description of panel c, “circles represent mean EE per time point” should have been “circles represent mean RER per time point”; and in the description of panels d–f,h, “Left graph indicates representative 24-h period (circles represent mean EE per time point” should have been “Left graph shows representative 24-h period (circles represent mean values per time point”. In the Extended Data Fig. 10 legend, “All p values in this figure obtained using unpaired two tailed t-test” should have been “All p values except (b) obtained using unpaired, two-tailed t-test”; in the description of panel c, “circles represent mean EE per time point” should have been “circles represent mean RER per time point”; and in the description of panels d–f, “Left graph shows representative 24-h period (circles represent mean EE per time point” should have been “Left graph shows representative 24-h period (circles represent mean values per time point”. These mistakes were due to typographical errors introduced during generation of the figure legends and the table; the statistics displayed in the figures and table were carried out using the correct numbers. Thus, the validity of the results and conclusions is unaffected. These corrections have been made to the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

Nintendo seems intent on letting The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time stay in the Switch 2 spotlight this year, so Pokémon fans still don't know when they'll be able to play Game Freak's next major RPG. Honestly, Pokémon Winds and Waves has been in a full-on information drought since the release of the reveal trailer back in early 2026. Well, there's at least one thing fans have to look forward in the realm of pocket monsters now, and it's happening sooner than anyone expected.

While you won't be able to play Pokémon Winds and Waves in the near future, one thing you can do beginning on Dec. 5 is purchase plushies based on Browt, Pombon and Gecqua. The grass, fire, and water starters have all been faithfully recreated in toy form, so you can make the arduous decision of which monster to pick well ahead of the actual game's release date.

In a recent development, perhaps it would help to know a little about each critter? Browt, for instance, is remarked to use photosynthesis to run around energetically — but The Pokémon Company cautions that the grass starter is kinda clumsy. The Shiba Inu-like Pombon apparently has heat-generating organsyet is one of the more affable monsters in the group. And finally, there's Gecqua, who is the most cunning monster of the three.

Sources indicate that here's a better look at each individual Winds and Waves starter plushie. Each one matches its starter’s appearance in the next-gen Pokémon game's reveal trailer to a T​​​​​​​.

Here's the fine print: As of right now, these plushies are only confirmed for Pokémon Center stores in Japan. Given the excitement around the game, it's probably just a matter of time before The Pokémon Company brings the starter plushies overseas as well.

It has been revealed that until then, and despite the information blackout from Game Freak, Pokémon fans still have lots to chew on. Leakers with access to internal documents from a 2024 information breach have steadily revealed unannounced details about Winds and Waves, including the apparent next professor, latest mechanics, Pokémon types, evolutions, and gym leaders, and map details.

And if that's not enough, the year has seen an explosion of fresh Pokémon fan games that might tide over players until Game Freak or TPC give us more to work with.

While many fans have enjoyed seeing their story play out from both perspectives, GTA 5 actor Ned Luke has given his take on the series being called “washed up”.

During an interview with Dexerto’s Fall Damage, the actor gave a blunt response to anyone taking problem with Lucia’s role in Rockstar’s latest open-world outing.

According to recent reports, “Okay, Borg, whatever you say, you don’t interest me,” Luke replied, addressing the viewer by their username. He then questioned why having a female protagonist would be a problem in the first place.

“What is woke? Woke. Oh, why? Because they got a female protagonist,” Luke mentioned. “What do they call those guys that don’t like women? Ah, idiots. That’s what they call them. Idiots,” he continued.

It has been revealed that “Oh, we can’t have a female protagonist because they’re going woke. Oh, because they got a girl,” Luke said. “Okay. You know what, dude? That girl is so badass. She’s, she’s more badass than you could ever dream of being.”.

Luke previously defended Lucia in a January 2024 interview with IGN, where he shared the following:.

“You get a lot of these clowns out here going, ‘Rockstar’s going woke, they’re caving into the wokeness of the world,’” Luke added. “First of all, there’s been other female protagonists in the past, but not in something as huge as this.”.

Despite the discourse around the protagonists, GTA 6 is now the joint best-reviewed game of all-time and has reportedly made over $750 million in pre-orders alone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates.

Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding.

In the snapshot, the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission.

In a recent development, this brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft right now resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

This crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles, Blue Moon and Starship, respectively.

In a recent development, to prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to initiative and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

Following investigations by ABC News in Australia and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, the app has been removed from the App Store.

Additionally, the app developers noted that most user access ‘stimulating’ content on there to help with everyday tasks and learning, but others have dipped into the companionship side of things.

Timmer’s video put a focus on how trees reacted to the intense wind gusts, as well as how much vehicles struggled to deal with it too. “You can really see the wind here,” he mentioned at one point while driving an excavator. “Look at that!”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GTA 6 developer has thanked Rockstar Games for immortalizing his baby daughter in an in-game memorial after he and his wife lost her five months into the pregnancy.
  • Since GTA 6 launched on November 19, millions of players have been exploring Leonida, uncovering hidden secrets and Easter eggs scattered throughout Rockstar’s sprawling open world.
  • However, some of the game’s most meaningful discoveries have been deeply personal tributes to the loved ones of those who spent years developing it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 developer has thanked Rockstar Games for immortalizing his baby daughter in an in-game memorial after he and his wife lost her five months into the pregnancy.

Since GTA 6 launched on November 19, millions of players have been exploring Leonida, uncovering hidden secrets and Easter eggs scattered throughout Rockstar’s sprawling open world.

However, some of the game’s most meaningful discoveries have been deeply personal tributes to the loved ones of those who spent years developing it.

Rockstar lead game tools programmer Bradley Stone took to X to share footage of himself visiting a memorial bearing his daughter’s name, Evelyn Stone, alongside the date April 8, 2023.

“To our baby we lost at 5 months pregnancy, you have been forever memorialised and honoured,” he wrote.

“Thank you, Rockstar for giving us this place to remember our loved ones, to show this game was made by real people and thank you for all the support/care you gave me through my grief.”.

Stone explained that he and his wife had already experienced multiple miscarriages when a scan in 2023 revealed their baby had a severe case of spina bifida.

Sources indicate that after further examinations and consultations with doctors, the couple learned that their daughter would not survive. They were left facing a medical termination, with Stone’s wife having to endure nearly 24 hours of labor.

This was the darkest moment of our lives and I cannot put into words the strength and courage my wife demonstrated and I can only love her more for that.A few years of ups and downs and more sadness we were finally blessed with a beautiful baby girl.

“We cried and held each other close as she delivered the baby,” he recalled. “The next hardest part was leaving the hospital without our baby. This still breaks me to this day.”.

Stone described the experience as the “darkest moment” of their lives, praising his wife’s strength and courage. He also revealed that, following several more years of ups and downs, the couple had welcomed a baby girl.

“To the baby we lost, we named you Evelyn,” he wrote. “You will forever be in our hearts.”.

Stone isn’t the only Rockstar employee whose loved ones have been immortalized in GTA 6. Fellow developer Matt Green previously revealed that his late mother, Bev, had been honored at the memorial just north of Hamlet.

While GTA 6 continues to shatter records around the world, the memorial serves as a touching reminder of the people behind the game and the loved ones they lost along the way.

  • After all, GTA 6 has more than 350 places where you can stop for a snack or a meal, from expensive fine-dining experiences, to farmers market stalls, to hole-in-the-wall fish sandwich shops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are countless ways to spend your time in Grand Theft Auto 6. You can scoop up pricey bundles of cocaine in a seaplane, do deadlifts to get sick gains, and scuba dive to discover marine life and lost pirate treasure. You can steal an elderly woman's mobility scooter and go to a yard sale to find cool vintage T-shirts. But sadly, one thing you cannot do is savor a delicious meal, whether it's on a solo outing or even on a date night with Jason and Lucia. GTA 6 has a vast, deep world with astonishing attention to detail in almost every capacity. But there's one area where the game comes up surprisingly short — the food.

In a recent development, in the early hours of GTA 6, you'll mostly be downing protein bars, apples, and various bagged snacks from the cupboard in Jason's Key Lento bungalow. It makes sense that these quick snacks aren't rendered in vivid detail — they don't have to be. That said, I was hoping that the game's many restaurants would show us something a little more elaborate.

After all, GTA 6 has more than 350 places where you can stop for a snack or a meal, from expensive fine-dining experiences, to farmers market stalls, to hole-in-the-wall fish sandwich shops. But sadly, pretty much every meal in the game kinda plays out like this. Yes, you can see Jason is clearly eating a hamburger, but the overall effect is not very different from tossing a protein bar down your pie hole.

Obviously, GTA 6 is not Cooking Mama. It is not a game that aspires to be "about food" in any way. Then again, there are plenty of non-food games that feature mouthwatering culinary creations that stick in your memory long after you've finished playing. Consider these examples from Final Fantasy 15, Unicorn Overlord, and Yakuza 0:.

Industry observers note that we know that Rockstar is capable of creating extremely detailed food — the Prairie Box combo from in-game fast food spot Chaco's is a precarious Jenga tower of floppy deli meats, an unholy Arby's nightmare given life. And even if food doesn't serve any particular gameplay function — like granting short-term stat buffs or opening up new dialogue — it's still fun to discover all the different creations. It feels like a missed opportunity to further explore GTA 6's riff on southern Florida, because Miami in particular has such a unique food scene. Let me get up close and personal with a pile of ropa vieja in Little Cuba! Let me savor some overpriced sushi on the main drag in Ocean Beach! Let me pick up a massive box of greasy Chinese with Cal for one of our gaming sessions. Heck, even the Rusty Anchor in Key Lento looks like the kind of place that would make a bangin' coconut shrimp plate.

You can make Jason and Lucia overweight in GTA 6, so why not let players enjoy it? A diet that consists primarily of protein bars and apples is no way to live.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to Durham Regional Police, officers responded to reports of a break-in at approximately 2:55 AM.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police in Canada are searching for at least three suspects after thieves crashed a stolen SUV through the front of a video game store before escaping in a waiting getaway vehicle.

The incident occurred in the early hours of November 26, just one week after the release of GTA 6, at We Got Gamez in Whitby, Ontario, leaving the business temporarily closed as its owners assess the damage.

According to Durham Regional Police, officers responded to reports of a break-in at approximately 2:55 AM.

Sources indicate that two suspects exited a black SUV after driving it through the storefront before fleeing in a second vehicle. Police later confirmed that the SUV used in the break-in had been stolen.

Industry observers note that the store was unoccupied at the time, and no injuries were reported. Authorities have not disclosed what merchandise was taken or its value.

In a series of Instagram posts, We Got Gamez shared its devastation over the incident but promised customers that the business would bounce back.

“Folks this is getting out of hand. Last night our Whitby Location was violated and broken into,” the store wrote.

A post shared by We Got Gamez (@wegotgamez1).

The owners estimate that the location will remain closed for 10 to 14 days as they clean up, account for missing merchandise, replace fixtures, and ensure the building is structurally safe for customers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor.
  • Recent findings suggest that the picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek.
  • The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor.

Recent findings suggest that the picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic.

The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower. The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet, which broke apart in the 1850s.

In a recent development, when Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm. This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour.

Recent findings suggest that not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible.

But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name).

Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors.

In 2011, astronomers announced that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She right now lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We might have to stop saying something sold like hotcakes and start saying something sold like Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar's latest has sold about as well as we expected, with estimates after only one week putting sales at over 50 million copies. That number will only go up in the weeks and months to come, especially if a new GTA Online mode and a PC version are eventually announced, as rumored.

In a recent development, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics, GTA 6 has sold 53 million copies in the week following the game's release on Nov. 19. That equates to $4.7 billion in revenue. By comparison, GTA 5 only sold 29 million copies in its entire first month. (It has since gone on to sell more than 230 million copies.) Other stats from the report reveal that nearly 7 million players have logged more than 50 hours in the game, with around 250,000 logging more than 100 hours.

The report also states that GTA 6 had an impact on sales for some of 2026's other major releases. On PlayStation, sales of several games (including 007 First Light​​​​​​​, Resident Evil Requiem, and Marvel's Wolverine) fell 34% during the week of GTA 6's release. ​​​​​​​Alinea Analytics points out​​​​​​​ that this isn't all GTA 6's fault, as typical sales decay for these titles was also in full swing. Interestingly, sales did actually go up slightly in the week before the game's release, possibly because some players​​​​​​​ ​​​​​​​bought a PS5 and picked up a game or two​​​​​​​ to hold them over until GTA 6's release.​​​​​​​.

Of the more than 50 million copies of GTA 6 sold, more than 75% were sold for PlayStation 5.​​​​​​​ The report also indicates that Xbox sales have continued to decline​​​​​​​ in the days following the game's release. This suggests​​​​​​​ that Rockstar and PlayStation's marketing deal has been a massive success. Prior to the game's release, GTA 6 had been heavily promoted as playing best​​​​​​​ on Sony's console. Granted, PlayStation does presently hold roughly 75% of the console market, making GTA 6 sales roughly proportional to its market share​​​​​​​. Fresh off the success of GTA 6 on PlayStation 5, Sony has already struck a similar marketing deal with CD Projekt Red for future releases, including The Witcher 4.

PC players have been left out of the fun so far, with no official word on a PC release for GTA 6. That hasn't stopped hackers from trying to make their own, with builds making speedy progress after an Xbox executable file was leaked to the public, kick-starting a race to create an unofficial PC port​​​​​​​. Hopefully, we'll hear official word on a PC release and multiplayer sometime in 2027.​​​​​​​.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is now available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

#738. Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (999 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Space)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some constellations are like old friends.
  • It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting.
  • Sources indicate that but look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W.

It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination.

Sources indicate that but look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Massive Dipper/the Plough. It's gone.

In a recent development, nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn.

Recent findings suggest that late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3.

Sources indicate that this is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations, it circles the north celestial pole — a position presently held by Polaris, the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon.

According to recent reports, this gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract.

I'm going to observe Cassiopeia twice on the same evening this week, which is about as complicated as the experiment needs to get. The first time will be shortly after darkness falls. I'll find the W, note which way it seems to be pointing and use something fixed — a rooftop, tree or chimney — to give myself a rough reference for its position. I'll return to my backyard before bed, and see where the pattern has shifted. Cassiopeia's main stars are bright enough to survive urban and suburban light pollution, so you don't need a particularly dark sky or a telescope.

Industry observers note that while I'm gazing at Cassiopeia, I'll try to see the stars as they really are, and not just how they appear to us. Check out the distances of its stars from the sun:.

Recent findings suggest that only Caph and Ruchbah are within 100 light-years — the sun's local interstellar neighborhood. Does that destroy the very concept of Cassiopeia as a group of related stars? Cassiopeia, like all constellations, is a mirage, with a capital M.

According to recent reports, there's another reason I love Cassiopeia. Proxima Centauri, the closest star to our sun, lies just 4.24 light-years away. Travel there and look back towards our solar system, and our sun would appear as an extra star in Cassiopeia — effectively giving the constellation a sixth bright point. From a certain perspective, we are all Cassiopeians.

Sources indicate that the last few evenings of November bring back darker early-night skies as the moon wanes from full earlier in the week and rises progressively later. It will rise in the middle of the night as it reaches its last-quarter phase on Dec. 1. It's an ideal time to sweep a pair of binoculars across the rich star fields around Cassiopeia and Perseus. On the boundary between the two constellations is the Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884), one of the finest binocular sights in the entire northern sky. These two dense concentrations of young stars sit side by side against the richer background of the Milky Way. Under a dark sky, you can see it with the naked eye. M52, NGC 457 (the Owl Cluster) and NGC 663 are other clusters also worth seeking out in Cassiopeia.

Get outside about 45 minutes before sunrise on Monday, Nov. 30, and look high in the southern sky for a fitting month-ending finale. A 61%-lit waning gibbous moon will appear alongside brilliant Jupiter, reddish Mars and Regulus, the brightest star in Leo. Together, the four objects will trace a striking crescent spanning just over five degrees of sky — roughly the width of three fingers held at arm's length. It's a much tighter version of a similar arrangement visible on Nov. 2, with Jupiter by far the brightest point and the contrasting colors of Mars and blue-white Regulus adding to the spectacle. No equipment will be needed, though binoculars will help you get a close-up of this rather unusual conjunction.
