#616. At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2303 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Eurogamer)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for 16 years I've been watching the skies.
  • Faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch".
  • It has been revealed that okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for 16 years I've been watching the skies. It was 16 years ago, back in the first giddy rush of smartphone gaming, that I saw a 30-second trailer for a game set in space. It was a game about a comet, hurtling through the unknown. It wasn't clear what you'd do in this game, whether you'd control the comet itself or the space it moved through. It wasn't clear if this was some kind of arcade game, or a new spin on the endless runner, or even just a kind of cosmic sandbox. All I had was the comet and a name: Faraway. Faraway! I was captivated.

Faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch". Where is the edge of the galaxy? Oh, it's faraway. Where is the edge of the universe? Oh, there's nonesuch thing.

It has been revealed that okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time. It was being made by Steph Thirion, a musician and designer and, I sensed, many other things too. At the time Faraway was announced I'd just played his game Eliss, which was an early smartphone hit. In the absence of any more information on Faraway itself, I had to make do with that. Maybe Faraway would be a bit like Eliss?

According to recent reports, eliss itself, though? Oh, boy. This thing is beautiful, frantic, strange, compelling and indescribable. And think what that means, just for a second, for something to be both compelling and indescribable. I am driven to do these things, but I don't really know what these things are. I'm prodding little bits of colour around, maybe planets, maybe molecules? I am combining them, gathering them, turning them into something greater together than they are by themselves?

Last week I spoke to Thirion - as for why, well, we will get to that - and at the start I asked him about Eliss, about how it felt to make a game that was so hard to put into words, and if he actually had any words for it himself.

"I love that question," he laughs. "I guess I would say that for Eliss, it was all about that interaction of moving things, moving those little circles with each of your fingers individually." He pauses, thinking back. "It's not something I had envisioned. I was programming, and I was basically testing touch controls because I was trying to build a different game. But then I was playing with that [stuff]. I was like: that feels really nice. Can I build a game around that? So I guess there is something beyond language about that interaction. I was attracted to it in that way. It wasn't rational. It was a feeling. It feels good.".

It's both thrilling and slightly melancholic to think back to the days of Eliss. Apps were in ascendence, but nobody fully understood them yet. There weren't yet consultants or established monetisation pathways. There wasn't even much agreement on the best ways to approach the touchscreen. Eliss and other weird, memorable, hard-to-talk-about games were all part of this Cambrian explosion. You'd get up in the morning and check socials and there was a new game everyone was enthusing about. There was a new world to get lost in.

"I would say that's true even outside of mobile," Thirion tells me. "Just indies in general. There was a lot of excitement going around and a lot of eyeballs. What are people gonna think about next?" He takes a long breath. "It felt like there's a lot of opportunity for new things and new ideas, and people were excited about that. Everything was set up for innovation. It felt like I was part of something.".

Recent findings suggest that this is the world that Faraway and its comet first emerged from, streaking across a night sky in which any kind of discovery felt possible. "The real genesis was actually just before Eliss," Thirion states. "I was really spending a lot of time thinking about a possible career in video games. I was an interaction designer and programmer doing interactive experiences, mostly for advertising.

"And for some reason, the iPhone was the thing that made me think I could do something on my own, and what I'd like to do is probably video games. So I was I was thinking a lot about that, maybe obsessively, to the point where there was a night that I was in the countryside in France and just looking at the stars and thinking: it would be great to have a video game where you can fly in the sky that I'm looking at, in this 2D firmament, right? That was it.".

The next step towards Faraway came at GDC in 2010, with a call for games that could be controlled with a single button. "I started prototyping," Thirion notes. "I tried a few things, and I had this idea of using this kind of physics-y thing about swinging around stars. It actually worked pretty rapidly.".

Industry observers note that then? Sixteen years pass. What was happening during this time?

Recent findings suggest that it's a long answer with, perhaps, a short answer buried inside it. Let's deal with the long answer first.

"It's not like I worked 16 years on this game," Thirion laughs. He explains that the first prototype was begun in 2010 for the GDC one-button competition. It was playable by March. "That was basically at the beginning," he says. "I was like: This is a very simple game, and I'm just going to put it out in a couple months.".

In a recent development, and after that? "I started to have greater ambitions, and then life happened," he claims. He didn't work on the game for seven years, and then Annapurna Interactive found him and asked him to return to Faraway, offering support. "And so, after that, the journey was to turn [the game] into an audiovisual experience.

Recent findings suggest that "And so I started doing an audiovisual experience, but it was still aesthetically like Ellis: low-resolution pixel art. I had the ambition of taking it to a different language. I basically wanted to make the jump from procedural low-resolution to procedural infinite resolution!" He ended up with a very smooth, almost vector-like aesthetic. It looks beautiful, but it came at a price. "That took a lot of effort," he notes. "Also to make it performant? That required a rewrite of the game into a completely latest engine. It was a new language for me as well, so I had to learn this new language.".

According to recent reports, all of this is extremely convincing, as are a hundred other bumps in the road. It makes sense. I've written about games for twenty years, and my sense is that game development is hard, and that it takes time.

It has been revealed that but there's something else Thirion says. And this makes me wonder if part of the truth as to why Faraway took so long to make is actually a lot simpler, and a lot more human.

In a recent development, "I was thinking a lot about Tetris," Thirion says. "I had just started making video games, and I thought a lot about Tetris because it's a very simple rule set that seems to be compelling whether you're two hours in or 1000 hours in, right? And that's like kind of a rare thing.

Industry observers note that "And at the time we were talking about: are game's art and so on. And I was like, man, to me, Tetris is art. It does something almost impossible. At least now I look at it and I think it does something almost impossible. But at the time, I was like, well, why are games growing in complexity and quantity instead of staying simple and going deep? And so, I was really asking myself the question: where can I find that balance of just being compelling at any skill level with a very minimal rule set, and that kind of took me into this rabbit hole of experimentation.".

According to recent reports, it's hard for me not to sympathise with this. Thirion had worked on something for a very short period of time, and he'd found something that felt - well, that felt kind of eternal, boundless in there. A comet swinging through space with one touch controls! What could be more pleasing, more engaging than that? But with that came a lot of challenges. It wasn't just a question of what to add. Adding things would be easy. It was how to create a deep experience that didn't overburden the whole idea and make you lose sight of its simplicity. Put like that, 16 years doesn't seem like a very long time at all.

That's his journey, anyway. As for mine? Well, 16 years is a lot of time if you aren't a comet. I continued writing about games. I got married. I had a daughter. My daughter grew up and went to primary school and is now at secondary school. The whole games industry transformed and then transformed again and is transforming again now. I started learning to swim!

And throughout all this, every few years I would email Thirion and ask if he was ready to talk yet, whether he was ready to talk about Faraway and whether his comet was still blazing somewhere in some private night sky.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year I looked him up once more and saw a new trailer. It was short again, and there was the comet I had seen all those years ago. And then, at the end, there was a date. A release date. That comet was finally swinging by the earth.

In a recent development, and so a few weeks ago I loaded up a game I had been waiting to play for 16 years and which I realised, as I paged through the early screens, that I still knew absolutely nothing about. Well. Do you want to hear about it? Or would you rather discover it for yourself?

Recent findings suggest that I would rather you discover it for yourself. But if you don't want to, listen:.

In a recent development, faraway is a game about a comet. The comet is racing through space, and you are the comet, even if you only control it indirectly. Touch a button - there is only one button - and you can bind the comet to the gravity of a nearby star. Keep your finger pressed down on the button and you will remain gravitationally bound, which means you can use stars to adjust your course, your trajectory, your speed. Let go of the button and you're off again. Off into the depths of space. And out there, new stars await.

Recent findings suggest that from this simple interaction, Faraway builds a constellation of challenges that I find both simple to understand and - yes - incredibly difficult to adequately put into words. I'm not going to tell you too much, because I really want you to play this thing, but Faraway at its core is a bit like sewing, a bit like driving, a bit like counting and making shapes and a bit like desperately trying to stay alive. That's it. It's beautiful and serene, but it's also desperate. It's abstract and reliable and I find it extremely moving to play.

It has been revealed that more than anything, I think I love the feel of it. The steady arc of the comet bends and flexes beneath you as you push and hold the button. There's a thrilling sense of just about bending something elemental to your will. There's beauty to be found in timing your escape from an orbit, and the orbit paths themselves, when you press and hold the button and newly introduced trajectories announce themselves, have a Spirograph delight to them. Does it really matter what you do in a game when it has stuff like this in it?

According to recent reports, now, I am weird, and I spend a lot of my time on Earth thinking about the wilds of space and the vast distances and the places we will never get to see and all the things that are so hostile to life that we wouldn't survive a second in their presence. I think about the Wow Signal and the Great Attractor and Tabby's Star and all of that beautiful, terrifying stuff. It calms me down. It puts my own problems in perspective. It's probably the closest thing I get to any kind of religious observance.

And Thirion thinks about this stuff too. I know because, after 16 years, I asked him. "It really resonates with me," he says. "I do spend a lot of time thinking about [the universe]. I don't know why there is anything at all, right? And the fact that we can never answer that question, and the fact that there are many questions that we'll probably never be able to answer.

Sources indicate that "But I also spend a lot of time looking at the clouds and looking at the grass and how the light hits the drops of water. There's so much beauty. We're given so much beauty by the universe, and we're so lucky.

Industry observers note that "And the game comes out of that a little bit. I don't know exactly what the game is about, but maybe you could interpret it as: why am I here? Why is life so short? Why is life so long?".

He laughs. "I often ask myself: why is there anything at all? And how is it so beautiful?".

  • A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

In a recent development, that isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

"The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University mentioned in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events.".

The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy, a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.

It has been revealed that responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years,.

In a recent development, they determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits.

Sources indicate that "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years.".

An crucial clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star.

It has been revealed that when Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025.

One of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Massive Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier.

This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass.

Recent findings suggest that "It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Big and Little Bao," Karambelkar stated. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries.".

In a recent development, the team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #611. How to navigate the holiday party season while sober

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2431 w)

How to navigate the holiday party season while sober

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.
  • When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.
  • In a recent development, “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” says the 45-year-old communications professional.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles. “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” claims the 45-year-old communications professional. “My job is about bringing people together. And when people are brought together, there’s always alcohol on the table.” Read, who says she was never much of a drinker to begin with, started limiting her consumption to a drink or two at work-related events about five years ago. As a mother of four, however, she found that even a small amount was more trouble than it was worth. “My kids are really young. I have to be up early in the morning, and it was starting to affect my sleep,” she says. “It just had downstream impacts that I really wasn’t appreciating.” Read says her colleagues supported her decision to give up alcohol completely, but says it’s still hard to navigate professional situations with upcoming people, like networking events. “I had trepidation about being fully sober because I knew it was an awkward conversation to have,” she says. “Sometimes I will hold a glass of sparkling water instead of champagne to not feel like I need to explain myself.” Read isn’t the only one who occasionally finds strategies to avoid conversations about her sobriety. According to a recent survey by the Boca Recovery Center, which operates addiction treatment centers in Florida, Indiana, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, 39% of Americans who abstain from alcohol hide their sobriety at work and 30% fake it to blend in—like drinking sparkling water from a champagne flute. And 13% have skipped a work event, celebration, or date to avoid the topic altogether. Given that more than half of sober Americans have been questioned, pressured, or teased about their decision not to consume alcohol, according to the survey, it is perhaps no surprise that 58% hide it from at least some people in their lives, and that 13% haven’t told anyone. “The holidays make this harder, as events tend to be based around drinking,” says Alison Tarlow, a licensed clinical psychologist who is the chief clinical officer at Boca Recovery Center. “Those hiding their sobriety are managing a drink, an excuse and a conversation all at once—which is socially exhausting in a setting that is supposed to be fun and relaxed.” Stigma remains even as more Americans go sober More Americans are choosing to go alcohol-free for a wide variety of reasons, though taboos related to addiction and mental health remain. According to the survey, one in four Americans have experimented with alcohol-free or reduced-drinking challenges; half of these cite physical or mental health-related reasons, compared with 10% who were recovering from addiction. Against this backdrop, younger generations appear less likely than others to hide their sobriety. According to the survey, only 5% of Gen Z keep it a secret, compared with 12% of millennials and 20% of Gen Xers. But these younger Americans also face the most outside stigma, as 68% of sober Gen Zs have faced questioning, pressure, or teasing compared with 49% of older sober Americans. “Telling people tends to involve fielding questions, which is generally off-putting to those who made such a personal decision,” says Tarlow. “Sobriety is a complex and sensitive decision, and people want to choose who hears about it and when.” Navigating the holiday party season without alcohol The holidays can be an especially challenging time for those who are looking to stay sober. Between personal and professional events, family and financial obligations ramping up, and work responsibilities starting to dwindle, many are left without some of the support systems, practical reasons, or reminders that help them maintain sobriety. Though they may feel judged for ordering an alcohol-free alternative, 93% of Americans say they would not think less of a coworker who skips alcohol at a work event, according to the survey. “The judgment sober people anticipate is usually harsher than what their peers tend to think,” says Tarlow. While colleagues may ask questions, she emphasizes that those who choose sobriety don’t need to explain themselves. “’I’m not drinking tonight’ is perfectly fine,” Tarlow says. “These events are meant to be fun, so focus on enjoying yourself, not others’ expectations. But, if pressure builds, there’s no shame in taking a break or leaving.” Coming up with excuses for not drinking can be exhausting and dishonest, says Phillip Barbb, an executive coach who specializes in sobriety. “You don’t want to feel like you have to have 25 conversations where you’re lying at the holiday party,” he says. “Creating this false narrative for yourself can weigh on you, because you’re building a gap between yourself and others.” Instead, Barbb, who has been sober for almost 19 years himself, suggests preparing a short explanation in advance that feels authentic and genuine, like, “I’m doing it for health reasons,” or “I decided I wanted to try not drinking this holiday season.” Some may also find it helpful to create a practical reason for staying sober to help them through workplace holiday events, like being a designated driver or making an early-morning commitment for the following day. Those trying to stick to their sobriety goals can also enlist the support of a colleague, date, or friend, though Barbb warns that these people shouldn’t be made responsible for someone else’s choices. “It is no one else’s responsibility to keep me sober or to keep me out of bad situations,” he says. “What I do think is cool is saying, ‘I want to go to the event, I don’t want to drink, so I may have a moment or two where I need to pull you aside to just talk or vent.’” How employers can offer more inclusive holiday parties for sober staff With so many Americans experimenting with sobriety—and so many hiding it from their colleagues—organizations will inevitably strategy holiday parties for attendees who are abstaining from alcohol, whether the organization knows it or not. So it’s important for employers to consider ways they can make the environment more inclusive for workers who don’t want to drink. When a holiday party’s primary activity is consumption, it can make those who are going sober stand out. That is why employers are encouraged to include other activities, like bowling, an escape room, or mini golf. Choice of venue can also play a role, as an event held at a bar or club may create more anxiety—and discourage more from attending—than one held at an activity venue or restaurant. “If you’re hosting an event, you do have a responsibility to offer more than just beer and wine so that people can feel comfortable,” Barbb adds. “If you’re offering signature drinks, do a version without alcohol.” Workplace cultures are often set at the top, meaning it’s up to leaders to model responsible behavior and signal inclusivity for sober attendees. “It’s not anybody’s job—nor is it their right—to pry into the lives of their employees. But you should still make sure that you’re creating environments that are safe for people to be in,” Barbb says. “For executives and leaders, your responsibility for your people continues even outside of work hours.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DanganronpaParanormasightSpike ChunsoftSquare Enix.

In a recent development, it could be argued thatÂ Grand Theft Auto V became such a long-running phenomenon thanks to the success of GTA Online and its popularity as a game with streamers. Grand Theft Auto VI has also been dominating on streaming websites since its release, alongside beingÂ the biggest gaming launch of all time. Given this, you might assume all would agree that streaming is great for gaming, but there are still some Japanese developersâespecially in the realms of visual novels and story-driven gamesâwho feel differently. In a country where the legal landscape for streaming is very different to that seen in the West, not all agree on how to approach the topic, as seen during a conversation between the producers of two recent hits of the genre in Japan: Paranormasightâs Kazuma Oushu and Danganronpaâs Shohei Sakakibara.

Even Nintendo once tried to enforce such restrictions globally. The argument is that streaming could hurt sales, especially for story-driven titles, despite there being little evidence to support this. At Japanese gaming developer conference CEDEC+Kyushu, as reported by Gamer (via Automaton Media), the creators behind Danganronpa and Paranormasight debated the merits of such restrictions, with differing opinions. Danganronpa‘s Sakakibara sees such limitations as an obvious block against destroying the core appeal of a murder mystery by giving away the answers. âIf you find out who the culprit is beforehand, half the fun is gone,â he explains. âWho would want to play a mystery when they already know the culprit? I absolutely donât want to take that experience away from players.â.

Yet 2023’s Square Enix visual novel Paranormasaight is arguably proof that spoilers may not hurt sales, even for story-driven games. This mystery adventure game limited streamers from sharing just the final chapter online, and lifted this after less than a month. Oushu noted that streaming helped raise awareness for the game. âThe people who are going to buy the game will buy it even if all the tricks get revealed in a video,â he claimed.

In a recent development, it can especially help in long-term sales after a gameâs launch, Oushu argued. People attracted to the unique visuals and setting would forget about the specific spoilers but remember being intrigued by its world by the time it went on sale, he suggested. They would see it as âan interesting game that, if it goes on sale, Iâll play itâ, Oushu added, boosting its success in the long run. Heavier restrictions, he argued, wonât allow players that sense of discovery. It also helped sales for the more recently released sequel: some who watched videos of the first game would go on to play the sequel themselves, without watching streaming content beforehand.

The debate on game streaming has mostly been settled. Today, Twitch is one of the biggest online video platforms, Nintendo lifted restrictions many years ago, and influencers are a key part of promoting almost every modern game released today. But there is still the argument it could hurt smaller and niche titles, and both producers acknowledged the relatively lower prices of their games as factors in their success despite streaming.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what happens when the world’s most valuable technology company becomes a target for foreign intelligence?
  • What happens when the world’s most valuable technology firm becomes a target for foreign intelligence?
  • From the inner workings of the CIA to China’s pursuit of American technology, these eight books explore the world of spies and secrets, where information can be every bit as valuable as the technology itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what happens when the world’s most valuable technology company becomes a target for foreign intelligence? That question has taken on latest urgency at Nvidia, where allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, its founder, sparked an independent investigation and contributed to his temporary departure as CEO. The unfolding controversy has brought fresh attention to the high-stakes struggle for technological power. From the inner workings of the CIA to China’s pursuit of American technology, these eight books explore the world of spies and secrets, where information can be every bit as valuable as the technology itself. Learn something new every day with “Book Bites,” 15-minute audio summaries of the latest and greatest nonfiction. Get started by downloading the Next Big Idea App today! The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip By Stephen Witt How did Nvidia become one of the most powerful companies in the world? Stephen Witt tells the remarkable story of Jensen Huang and his rise from ambitious entrepreneur to the man at the center of the AI revolution. It’s a revealing look at the company whose chips have become some of the most coveted technology on the planet, and why control over them matters far beyond Silicon Valley. Listen to our podcast interview with Stephen in the app or on YouTube, and purchase on Bookshop or Amazon. The Great Heist: China’s Epic Campaign to Steal America’s Secrets By David Shedd & Andrew Badger The battle for technological supremacy isn’t always fought in laboratories or boardrooms. Sometimes, it’s fought in the shadows. Drawing on decades of intelligence experience, David Shedd and Andrew Badger expose China’s sweeping campaign to steal American innovations and secrets, revealing how espionage has become a powerful weapon in the struggle for global dominance. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by David and Andrew. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. Spies, Lies, and Algorithms: The History and Future of American Intelligence By Amy Zegart Forget what Hollywood has taught you about spies. The real world of intelligence is stranger, more complicated, and increasingly shaped by technology. The Stanford scholar Amy Zegart takes readers inside the CIA and America’s intelligence agencies to reveal how espionage actually works, why intelligence failures happen, and how the digital revolution is rewriting the rules of spying. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by Amy. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. The Secret Life of Secrets: How Our Inner Worlds Shape Well-Being, Relationships, and Who We Are By Michael Slepian Not all secrets are matters of national security. Some are deeply personal, and they can be just as powerful. The psychologist Michael Slepian draws on years of research to explore why we keep secrets, what they do to our minds, and how the things we conceal can shape our relationships and our sense of self. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by Michael. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. Sell Like A Spy: The Art of Persuasion from the World of Espionage By Jeremy Hurewitz What can a CIA operative teach you about winning someone’s trust? Quite a lot, it turns out. ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the greatest tech-related purchases I’ve made of late is a product with no technology in it.I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it.
  • One of the greatest tech-related purchases I’ve made of late is a product with no technology in it.I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it.
  • Recent findings suggest that I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the greatest tech-related purchases I’ve made of late is a product with no technology in it.I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it. That’s how I wound up with a 10-slot device organizer from a brand called MobileVision.I almost ordered the seven-slot version instead, but promptly realized there’d be no trouble filling a few more spaces. I also snaked a USB-C cable up behind the organizer, so I can always be charging something.This simple accessory has been a revelation, and not just because it helped tidy up my office. In my head it also creates a default place to store everything, which means one thing less to think about. This must be what actually organized people feel like all the time, I guess.This story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.The device organizer isn’t the only way I’ve been trying to tidy up my gadget situation. Here are a handful of other solutions I’ve accumulated over the years:Retractable chargersI mentioned retractable charging cables back in my year-end list of favorite tech things. The Baseus charging station on my desk (seemingly discontinued, though I’m happy with it) has a built-in cable I can pull out when my phone needs a top-up, while a separate Anker charger in the living room has a pair of retractable cables for the kids’ iPads. Both have cut down on the number of cables constantly dangling about.Charge connector adapters (with lanyards)While I’d love it if all my devices charged via USB-C, I’ve got a few stragglers that depend on Apple’s Lightning connector or the aging Micro USB standard. Instead of keeping separate cables around for these devices, I’ve decluttered by using little charging adapters that snap onto any USB-C connector.The key is to find ones with built-in lanyards, so they can hang onto to a USB-C cable even when they’re not plugged in. I use these Lightning-to-USB-C adapters for the aforementioned kids’ iPads, and have finally gotten around to buying a similar set for Micro USB.Cable tiesI am forever hoarding the velcro ties that sometimes come with charging cables, so I can use them to bunch various charging and data cables together. Huge packs of them are also available for cheap. (Alternatively, you can install cable hiders to keep things extra clean, but I’m reluctant to head down that rabbit hole.)Docking stations and standsPerhaps you noticed the lack of an iPad Pro to go with the Magic Keyboard in my organizer. That’s because it has its own magnetic charging stand in front of my desk, where I often use the iPad to take interview notes.Beyond that, I bought this cheap 3-in-1 Anker charging stand years ago, and it remains a nightstand fixture both at home and on the road. It works with any phone and earbuds with wireless charging, and you can snake a third charging cable through the USB-A port underneath. (Ostensibly, it’s for Apple Watches, but I’ve used it for other things as well.) I’ve also got a Steam Deck docking station that keeps it fully charged.I’m not saying you need to go on a massive organizational spree right now, but over time these little improvements have brought some much-needed order to my device empire. Perhaps they’ll give you some ideas of your own.Alternatively, you might just be thinking that I have too many gadgets sitting around to begin with. But that is a problem for another day.This story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it. That’s how I wound up with a 10-slot device organizer from a brand called MobileVision.

I almost ordered the seven-slot version instead, but rapidly realized there’d be no trouble filling a few more spaces. I also snaked a USB-C cable up behind the organizer, so I can always be charging something.

This simple accessory has been a revelation, and not just because it helped tidy up my office. In my head it also creates a default place to store everything, which means one thing less to think about. This must be what actually organized people feel like all the time, I guess.

It has been revealed that this story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the device organizer isn’t the only way I’ve been trying to tidy up my gadget situation. Here are a handful of other solutions I’ve accumulated over the years:.

Sources indicate that I mentioned retractable charging cables back in my year-end list of favorite tech things. The Baseus charging station on my desk (seemingly discontinued, though I’m happy with it) has a built-in cable I can pull out when my phone needs a top-up, while a separate Anker charger in the living room has a pair of retractable cables for the kids’ iPads. Both have cut down on the number of cables constantly dangling about.

Industry observers note that while I’d love it if all my devices charged via USB-C, I’ve got a few stragglers that depend on Apple’s Lightning connector or the aging Micro USB standard. Instead of keeping separate cables around for these devices, I’ve decluttered by using little charging adapters that snap onto any USB-C connector.

The key is to find ones with built-in lanyards, so they can hang onto to a USB-C cable even when they’re not plugged in. I use these Lightning-to-USB-C adapters for the aforementioned kids’ iPads, and have finally gotten around to buying a similar set for Micro USB.

I am forever hoarding the velcro ties that sometimes come with charging cables, so I can use them to bunch various charging and data cables together. Huge packs of them are also available for cheap. (Alternatively, you can install cable hiders to keep things extra clean, but I’m reluctant to head down that rabbit hole.).

Industry observers note that perhaps you noticed the lack of an iPad Pro to go with the Magic Keyboard in my organizer. That’s because it has its own magnetic charging stand in front of my desk, where I often use the iPad to take interview notes.

Sources indicate that beyond that, I bought this cheap 3-in-1 Anker charging stand years ago, and it remains a nightstand fixture both at home and on the road. It works with any phone and earbuds with wireless charging, and you can snake a third charging cable through the USB-A port underneath. (Ostensibly, it’s for Apple Watches, but I’ve used it for other things as well.) I’ve also got a Steam Deck docking station that keeps it fully charged.

I’m not saying you need to go on a massive organizational spree right now, but over time these little improvements have brought some much-needed order to my device empire. Perhaps they’ll give you some ideas of your own.

Alternatively, you might just be thinking that I have too many gadgets sitting around to begin with. But that is a problem for another day.

Tech Report: A fashion reporter’s favorite things of 2026

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Being a fashion reporter can be a lot of fun.
  • Industry observers note that I’ll admit it.
  • Industry observers note that but what most people don’t realize is that the job also involves a lot of squinting at fiber-content labels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ll admit it. Being a fashion reporter can be a lot of fun. I get to sit across from some the most brilliant minds in the industry and peek at gorgeous collections seasons before they hit stores—long before they start shaping what we will wear. But what most people don’t realize is that the job also involves a lot of squinting at fiber-content labels. I’ve asked founders extremely nerdy questions about leather tanning methods. I’ve toured factories and tromped through cotton fields. Along the way, I come across many products. Over the course of a year, I wander through dozens of stores, wade through stacks of applications from brands hoping to land on our annual lists, and put bold newly introduced product claims to the test. Most of it is forgettable. But every so often, I come across something that I love: a clever jacket that is also beautiful, heels you can actually walk in all day, a pair of sneakers with a story so moving I still think about it months later. This list is the best of what I found in a year of poking, prodding, and road testing. If you’re shopping for someone who cares about style and quality, these are good bets. [Source Image: Resolute RGL] Every Stitch Tells a StoryResolute RGL, Najla in Olive Green, $350 Of the many products I reviewed this year, this is the one that made a biggest impression. Each Resolute sneaker carries a hand-embroidered panel of tatreez, the Palestinian cross embroidery that has passed down through generations. Each panel is stitched by a woman who lives in the villages in the South Hebron Hills of the West Bank. She chooses the pattern and colors herself, and a panel takes 14 to 24 hours to complete. The cooperative co-owns the company, and embroiderers are paid as soon as their panels are finished. The shoes themselves are lovely, with an olive suede upper, memory foam insoles, and recycled rubber soles. They’re made to order and take eight to 10 weeks to arrive, so plan ahead. [Source Image: Cole Haan] Light as a Feather, Tough Enough for a Nor’easterCole Haan, Grand Flex Fenella Buckle Lace-Up Waterproof Booties, $240 Most winter boots are heavy, adding weight as you trudge through the snow. Cole Haan has engineered these boots to be lightweight, but still set on a chunky lug sole that provides traction on icy sidewalks. They’re made from waterproof leather with sealed seams and a foam footbed that keep them cushy through a full day of walking. The buckle and laces give them a little edge, and a hidden ankle zip means you don’t have to do the laces again every time you leave the house. [Source Image: Parker Thatch] Mary Poppins Would Be Into ThisParker Thatch, Jack Tote in Leopard, $1,250 I am a person who carries too much: laptop, a novel, a snack, and a backup snack for my kids. The Jack allows overpackers to carry what they need for the day without looking like a duffel bag. It’s made from leopard-print hair-on cowhide with black leather trim and handles, and it fits a laptop with room to spare. There’s an interior zip pocket, two open pockets so your phone and glasses don’t get lost, and a snap closure. It’s the ideal gift for a professional woman in the market for a power bag. [Source Image: Lake] In-Law-Approved LoungewearLake, DreamModal Kimono Three-Piece Pants Set in Velvet Green Pencil Stripe, $168 The holidays involve lots of overnight guests, which can pose a dilemma. You want to be cozy, but you don’t want your in-laws to see you in your slinky nightgown or threadbare college T-shirt. Lake has many lounge sets. This one includes a wrap top with bell sleeves, a scoop-neck tank, and wide-leg pants with an elastic waist. It’s all made from a silky modal fiber, so it feels like you’re wearing pajamas but it looks like you’re in an outfit. The green and white stripe is festive without being kitschy. It’s machine washable, too. [Source Image: Margaux] Yes, You Can Walk in These HeelsMargaux, The Paloma Platform in Gold Nappa, $395 For years, most women assumed that “comfortable heels” is an oxymoron. Margaux is working hard to prove them wrong. The Paloma shoe has a 3.5-inch block heel, with a 1-inch platform, allowing you get the height without feeling unstable. There is plush foam padding under the sole and the straps are positioned so they don’t pinch. They’re handmade of nappa leather in Spain. I like the gold ones because they go with every holiday outfit. [Source Image: Maison de Sabré] Honey, I Shrunk the HandbagMaison de Sabré, The Mini Palais in Candy Plum, $675 Some nights call for nothing more than a phone, a lipstick, and a credit card. The Mini Palais is just substantial enough for these things, and its adjustable strap lets you wear it crossbody, on the shoulder, or in hand. The bags are also sustainable. Maison de Sabré skips conventional tanning, which is heavy on chemicals, in favor of DriTan, a waterless tanning technology. Each bag carries a serial number that allows you to trace it back to tanneries and farms in the Netherlands. And you can dress the bag up with adorable charms made from scraps of colorful leather discarded on the factory floor. [Source Image: Away] A Glamorous New Design from Away Away, The Aluminum Edge Carry-On, $428 Aluminum luggage has a certain glamour, but it’s heavy. Away’s new Aluminum Edge gives you a touch of aluminum on the frame and corners, but constructs the body out of a lighter polycarbonate shell that has a leather-like finish. It is full of luxurious touches, like champagne or nickel hardware. It closes with a lock, instead of a zipper, and it has a leather top handle. It comes in four colors, including a fun pink. [Source Image: Credo Beauty] Twelve Days of Clean BeautyCredo Beauty, Not Your Average Advent Calendar, $175 Credo, a retailer that stocks only nontoxic beauty brands, launched an Advent calendar full of 12 full-size bestsellers (worth $445 in products) inside a blue beauty case. Some of my favorite products inside include a Westman Atelier lipstick, Saie’s mascara, and Nécessaire’s hand cream. There’s no waste in this Advent calendar. You’ll carry the toiletry bag around for years to come. [Source Image: Minnow] Swimwear for a Winter EscapeMinnow, Women’s Marigold Floral V-Neck One Piece, $218, and Marigold Floral Pareo, $128 If you’re lucky enough to be headed somewhere warm over the holidays, or you’re already dreaming about next year’s beach trip, this is what I’d pack. Minnow is a resort brand that makes thoughtfully designed swimwear. This summery set provides substantial coverage, while staying put so you can enjoy the pool with your kids. The matching pareo means you can wear the outfit to your hotel’s buffet breakfast before lounging poolside. (And if the whole family is coming along, the suit can be coordinated with matching styles for everybody.) [Source Image: Overland] A Functional, Beautiful JacketOverland, Kylie Reversible Sheepskin Jacket, $1,195 If you read my coats roundup this fall, you’ll recognize this jacket, made by Overland, which has been making sheepskin coats since 1973. I’m bringing it back because of all the jackets I tested this year, this one stood out. One side is a sleek leather jacket that has a strip of shearling peeking out at the collar. If you flip it inside out, it transforms into a plush shearling jacket. The pockets work from either side. It’s built to last, too, since sheepskin can last a lifetime with proper care. [Source Image: White + Warren] A Blanket-Like ScarfWhite + Warren, Cashmere Travel Wrap in Antique Gold, $385 Cashmere scarves are a traditional holiday gift, since they’re something anybody can appreciate. But this one stands out. It’s made of 100% cashmere but at almost 7 feet long, it works as a scarf, an evening wrap, or a full-body blanket on a red-eye. It can squish into a tote bag, but when you wear it, it feels substantial. It comes in a rainbow of colors; my favorite is the antique gold. [Source Image: Assouline] For the Bag Obsessive Who Has EverythingAssouline, Fashionphile: The Book of Iconic Bags, $120 Here’s a gift for the bag obsessive. Fashionphile, the luxury resale platform, knows exactly which bags hold their value and why. It has teamed up with Assouline to produce a silk-covered, 280-page tome about the 25 most influential handbags of all time, from the Hermès Birkin to the Fendi Baguette and the Dior Saddle, plus newer icons from Bottega Veneta and Loewe. It has more than 200 illustrations that will be eye candy to fashionistas. [Source Image: ME+EM] Three Earrings in OneME+EM, Transformer Earrings, $495 This piece of jewelry magically transforms to suit your outfit. The earrings start as gold-plated studs for the office. Clip on the detachable pendant and they become drops for dinner. The pendant is double-sided, with black marbled resin on one side and gold on the other, so you can flip it to suit your mood or your outfit. They’re made in Italy, and they work as well with a turtleneck as with a cocktail dress.

The shoes themselves are lovely, with an olive suede upper, memory foam insoles, and recycled rubber soles. They’re made to order and take eight to 10 weeks to arrive, so initiative ahead.

Light as a Feather, Tough Enough for a Nor’easterCole Haan, Grand Flex Fenella Buckle Lace-Up Waterproof Booties, $240.

Industry observers note that most winter boots are heavy, adding weight as you trudge through the snow. Cole Haan has engineered these boots to be lightweight, but still set on a chunky lug sole that provides traction on icy sidewalks. They’re made from waterproof leather with sealed seams and a foam footbed that keep them cushy through a full day of walking. The buckle and laces give them a little edge, and a hidden ankle zip means you don’t have to do the laces again every time you leave the house.

Mary Poppins Would Be Into ThisParker Thatch, Jack Tote in Leopard, $1,250.

I am a person who carries too much: laptop, a novel, a snack, and a backup snack for my kids. The Jack allows overpackers to carry what they need for the day without looking like a duffel bag. It’s made from leopard-print hair-on cowhide with black leather trim and handles, and it fits a laptop with room to spare. There’s an interior zip pocket, two open pockets so your phone and glasses don’t get lost, and a snap closure. It’s the ideal gift for a professional woman in the market for a power bag.

In-Law-Approved LoungewearLake, DreamModal Kimono Three-Piece Pants Set in Velvet Green Pencil Stripe, $168.

According to recent reports, the holidays involve lots of overnight guests, which can pose a dilemma. You want to be cozy, but you don’t want your in-laws to see you in your slinky nightgown or threadbare college T-shirt. Lake has many lounge sets. This one includes a wrap top with bell sleeves, a scoop-neck tank, and wide-leg pants with an elastic waist. It’s all made from a silky modal fiber, so it feels like you’re wearing pajamas but it looks like you’re in an outfit. The green and white stripe is festive without being kitschy. It’s machine washable, too.

Yes, You Can Walk in These HeelsMargaux, The Paloma Platform in Gold Nappa, $395.

For years, most women assumed that “comfortable heels” is an oxymoron. Margaux is working hard to prove them wrong. The Paloma shoe has a 3.5-inch block heel, with a 1-inch platform, allowing you get the height without feeling unstable. There is plush foam padding under the sole and the straps are positioned so they don’t pinch. They’re handmade of nappa leather in Spain. I like the gold ones because they go with every holiday outfit.

Honey, I Shrunk the HandbagMaison de Sabré, The Mini Palais in Candy Plum, $675.

According to recent reports, some nights call for nothing more than a phone, a lipstick, and a credit card. The Mini Palais is just significant enough for these things, and its adjustable strap lets you wear it crossbody, on the shoulder, or in hand. The bags are also sustainable. Maison de Sabré skips conventional tanning, which is heavy on chemicals, in favor of DriTan, a waterless tanning technology. Each bag carries a serial number that allows you to trace it back to tanneries and farms in the Netherlands. And you can dress the bag up with adorable charms made from scraps of colorful leather discarded on the factory floor.

A Glamorous Upcoming Design from Away.

Away, The Aluminum Edge Carry-On, $428.

Aluminum luggage has a certain glamour, but it’s heavy. Away’s fresh Aluminum Edge gives you a touch of aluminum on the frame and corners, but constructs the body out of a lighter polycarbonate shell that has a leather-like finish. It is full of luxurious touches, like champagne or nickel hardware. It closes with a lock, instead of a zipper, and it has a leather top handle. It comes in four colors, including a fun pink.

Twelve Days of Clean BeautyCredo Beauty, Not Your Average Advent Calendar, $175.

Sources indicate that credo, a retailer that stocks only nontoxic beauty brands, released an Advent calendar full of 12 full-size bestsellers (worth $445 in products) inside a blue beauty case. Some of my favorite products inside include a Westman Atelier lipstick, Saie’s mascara, and Nécessaire’s hand cream. There’s no waste in this Advent calendar. You’ll carry the toiletry bag around for years to come.

Swimwear for a Winter EscapeMinnow, Women’s Marigold Floral V-Neck One Piece, $218, and Marigold Floral Pareo, $128.

It has been revealed that if you’re lucky enough to be headed somewhere warm over the holidays, or you’re already dreaming about next year’s beach trip, this is what I’d pack. Minnow is a resort brand that makes thoughtfully designed swimwear. This summery set provides substantial coverage, while staying put so you can enjoy the pool with your kids. The matching pareo means you can wear the outfit to your hotel’s buffet breakfast before lounging poolside. (And if the whole family is coming along, the suit can be coordinated with matching styles for everybody.).

A Functional, Beautiful JacketOverland, Kylie Reversible Sheepskin Jacket, $1,195.

If you read my coats roundup this fall, you’ll recognize this jacket, made by Overland, which has been making sheepskin coats since 1973. I’m bringing it back because of all the jackets I tested this year, this one stood out. One side is a sleek leather jacket that has a strip of shearling peeking out at the collar. If you flip it inside out, it transforms into a plush shearling jacket. The pockets work from either side. It’s built to last, too, since sheepskin can last a lifetime with proper care.

A Blanket-Like ScarfWhite + Warren, Cashmere Travel Wrap in Antique Gold, $385.

According to recent reports, cashmere scarves are a traditional holiday gift, since they’re something anybody can appreciate. But this one stands out. It’s made of 100% cashmere but at almost 7 feet long, it works as a scarf, an evening wrap, or a full-body blanket on a red-eye. It can squish into a tote bag, but when you wear it, it feels substantial. It comes in a rainbow of colors; my favorite is the antique gold.

For the Bag Obsessive Who Has EverythingAssouline, Fashionphile: The Book of Iconic Bags, $120.

Here’s a gift for the bag obsessive. Fashionphile, the luxury resale platform, knows exactly which bags hold their value and why. It has teamed up with Assouline to produce a silk-covered, 280-page tome about the 25 most influential handbags of all time, from the Hermès Birkin to the Fendi Baguette and the Dior Saddle, plus newer icons from Bottega Veneta and Loewe. It has more than 200 illustrations that will be eye candy to fashionistas.

Three Earrings in OneME+EM, Transformer Earrings, $495.

Recent findings suggest that this piece of jewelry magically transforms to suit your outfit. The earrings start as gold-plated studs for the office. Clip on the detachable pendant and they become drops for dinner. The pendant is double-sided, with black marbled resin on one side and gold on the other, so you can flip it to suit your mood or your outfit. They’re made in Italy, and they work as well with a turtleneck as with a cocktail dress.

The game found success by going against the trend for realism, evolving the anime expressionism and psychological ideas of prior games and putting them in a more appealing setting. It surpassed one million copies sold in just one year.â.

It was that success which led to the company pushing ahead with Persona 5 on Steam and doing more worldwide simultaneous releases. Nowadays, through remakes and concerts, the series has found multimedia success on a global scale, but the wait for a wholly upcoming entry goes on. However, the studio is actively refining its efforts to ensure that such long waits wonât become the norm. âPersona 6 is not the end goal,â Wada said. âWeâre putting in a lot of effort to ensure that fans wonât have to wait a long time for the next installment like before. To keep developing Persona into an even larger series, weâre also constantly thinking about concepts and story ideas that wonât disappoint expectations.â He clarified that faster development comes through greater collaboration between teams, and building systems that can be reused. There’s also an effort to pool veteran knowledge with series information that even the team has forgotten but fans can remember, all to ensure they donât need to remake elements with every entry.

Wada seems certain that, after so many years waiting for Persona 6, we wonât be waiting another decade for Persona 7. And who knows, if the rumored Persona 1 remake is real and can bridge the gap between releases, the wait may feel like nothing at all.

Industry News: Grand Theft Auto VI is a different kind of GTA — so it needed a different kind of ending

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (The Verge)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.
  • GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.
  • It has been revealed that in most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

It has been revealed that in most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience. After that’s done, there are usually still places you haven’t explored or side missions you left lingering. But Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t work quite the same way. Because of its storyline, which involves a couple trying to get out of the criminal life for good, that kind of ending didn’t really fit.

It has been revealed that “In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”.

This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson says the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

“Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”.

“You go back and have this open time again where you have the best single-player safehouse you’ve ever had in a GTA, with a garage full of supercars, a helipad, a gym, and all of the stuff you could ever want,” he states of the solution the studio landed on. “And you can spend as long as you want there. But you don’t have Tommy. So the characters don’t have the one thing that they wanted at the start. There’s the tension where you have to spend some extra time grinding to make some more money without knowing what it’s going to get you, and it plays out differently if you get that money.”.

One advantage of this structure is that it lets you try out different endings. GTA VI’s story can wrap up in multiple ways based on a variety of factors: how much money you have saved up, what kind of criminal you were throughout the game, and some key decisions you’re forced to make in the final moments. The upcoming postgame structure creates an opportunity to see some of the alternate ways the story can go. “There’s a large number of potential outcomes based on how you played it,” Nelson claims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One last month of 2026 brings two more waves of Xbox Game Pass titles to close out the year. Subscribers can once again look forward to some new arrivals in the Xbox Game Pass library, ranging from gruesome co-op action to wholesome adventures featuring helpful mice on a mission. These announcements typically come in two waves, with a sneak peek split between them, so while this list isn’t complete yet, we do know what you can expect in the first half of December. As usual, we’ll revision this page once Xbox reveals the full lineup for this first batch. For now, you can look forward to an eclectic mix of games, starting with The Outlast Trials. Released in 2024, it’s a co-op survival-horror game that throws a team of up to four players into a gauntlet of deadly trials, where evasion is key to victory. You can also play it solo, and if the onslaught of festive season cheerfulness is getting to you, then this will be a nice–but brutal–change of pace. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hCgiwsIUI4g If you’d prefer to focus on the coziness of the season, then Hela: Of Mice and Magic looks like a fun time. Set in a magical forest inspired by Scandinavian lands, the game follows a group of mice on a journey to help people, at the behest of an old witch who can’t make the trip herself. This is also a day-one release for Xbox Game Pass, and it’ll be joined by World of Tanks Blitz on the same day. On December 3, Freestyle Football 2 releases, bringing fast-paced, 5v5 multiplayer street soccer to Xbox and PC, and on December 14, you can grab Nubby’s Number Factory, a roguelite game all about making substantial numbers. Xbox Game Pass December Wave 1 Games December 1 The Outlast Trials (Cloud, Xbox Series X|S, and PC) — Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium, PC Game Pass Hela: Of Mice and Magic (Cloud, Xbox Series X|S, and PC) — Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass World of Tanks Blitz December 3 Freestyle Football 2 December 14 Nubby’s Number Factory If you missed it, November brought a solid selection of releases. The first wave added the dungeon-crawling roguelike deck-building game Dungeon Crawlers to more Game Pass tiers, along with Warhammer Survivors and John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando. The Game Pass library expanded further later in November, with some Paw Patrol fun for the kiddos, High on Life 2, and the pretty good long-distance stealth game Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 2.

In a recent development, after a national day of Thanksgiving, consumers have traditionally kicked off their holiday shopping on Black Friday. But are stores open and ready for it just one day after employees ate all that turkey? Here’s everything you need to know about what is open and closed on Black Friday. Is Black Friday a federal holiday? No, Black Friday is not a federal holiday, no matter what your shopaholic friends and family members may claim. Are banks open on Black Friday? Most banks are open on Black Friday, but some may have reduced hours because it is Thanksgiving week. Is the stock market open on Black Friday? Yes, both the Upcoming York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are open, but both institutions close early, at 1:00 p.m. ET. Perhaps all those buyers and sellers need a nap after eating some Thanksgiving leftovers. Is the Post Office open on Black Friday? Is mail delivered? Yes. U.S. Postal Service post office locations will be back in action on Black Friday. Mail will also be delivered. Are FedEx and UPS delivering on Black Friday? Yes, UPS is back to normal on Black Friday. Some FedEx locations may have modified hours. Additionally, on-call and drop box pickups may be early. Are schools open on Black Friday? Most schools will be closed for Thanksgiving break but it is a good practice to double-check with your student’s institution. Are restaurants open on Black Friday? Most restaurants will be open to help fuel shoppers for a long day of deal hunting. Call ahead, though, to double-check your favorite mom-and-pop joint. It might take some time off. Are retail stores open on Black Friday? Absolutely. Retail stores such as Best Buy, Walmart, Target, and others desperately want your business. Many sales have already started online ahead of the massive day. One notable exception is REI. For more than a decade, the outdoorsy store has promoted its “Opt Outside” initiative, remaining closed on Black Friday. Instead of shopping, it encourages people to take a hike, a walk, or do any outdoor activity. Are pharmacies open on Black Friday? Yes. Most pharmacies are open on Black Friday, including chains like CVS and Walgreens. Are grocery stores open on Black Friday? Yes, if you don’t have any Thanksgiving leftovers and need some grub, most grocery stores are open on Black Friday and happy to help. Membership-based stores like Costco and Sam’s Club will also be open.

#597. The simplest well-being strategy leaders overlook

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1412 w)

The simplest well-being strategy leaders overlook

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as leaders, we spend a lot of time thinking about employee well-being.
  • In a recent development, as leaders, we spend a lot of time thinking about employee well-being.
  • We know spending time in nature is good for us.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as leaders, we spend a lot of time thinking about employee well-being. I’ve found that supporting it often comes down to the everyday choices we make. That includes some of the simplest choices we tend to overlook. One of them is getting outside. We know spending time in nature is good for us. What’s striking is how hard it can be to do. The American Nature and Health Survey, which was supported by the REI Cooperative Action Fund in partnership with the Nature and Health Alliance, highlights this increasing disconnect. In the 2026 survey, Americans shared that nature is essential to their lives, yet we’re spending less time in it. A decade ago, 25% of respondents spent less than two hours a week in nature. Today, that number has nearly doubled to 45%. You can likely imagine why. Our lives are increasingly designed around convenience and screens. We can work, shop, connect, and entertain ourselves without ever stepping outside. Technology has made much of our lives easier and better, but it has also changed how we spend our time, often without us consciously making that choice.That matters because time in nature is linked to lower stress and better mental and physical health. And it doesn’t have to mean hours on the trail. Research suggests even 20 minutes outside can help us feel more centered, in mind and body. A RETAILER CLOSING ON BLACK FRIDAY For many people, there are real barriers to spending time outdoors, including access and safety. For others, it’s simply the competing demands of work and daily life. We still value nature, but too often, life makes it difficult to choose. That point has stuck with me as a business leader. There are plenty of things leaders can’t control. But we do have influence over how people spend their time at work and the conditions we create for people to do their best. With well-being, that means asking whether the way we work creates room for people to step away, recharge, and spend time outside. At REI Co-op, we’ve been exploring one version of that idea for more than a decade. In 2015, the co-op made an unusual choice for a retailer: We closed our stores on Black Friday, one of the most deeply ingrained traditions in American retail. We paid our employees to spend the day outside and encouraged customers to do the same. We called it Opt Outside. We didn’t tell employees how to spend the day or define what counted as “outside.” It could be a long hike, a walk through the neighborhood, time at a park with loved ones, or simply a quiet moment outdoors. The point was to create room for something that’s remarkably easy to push aside. MAKE CHOICES More than a decade since that first Opt Outside, I think there’s a leadership lesson in that choice, and it extends beyond REI. Not every tech giant should do what we did. As leaders, we all make choices about what we make room for. Those choices don’t have to be significant. Could your next one-on-one be a walk outside? Could a team gathering happen outdoors? Where in the workday could we make stepping outside, even for a few minutes, a little easier? These are small choices, but that’s the point. Supporting well-being and creating a better experience at work doesn’t always require another program or initiative. It starts with the everyday choices we make as leaders, and the things those choices make possible for others. CHOOSE TIME OUTSIDE This Black Friday, REI will once again close our stores and give our employees the day to spend outside. I’ll be doing the same, heading out for a hike with my family. One day outside doesn’t solve everything, and it’s not meant to. But after more than a decade of Opt Outside, at REI we still believe there’s value in choosing time outside. It has reinforced something for me about leadership: Our job is sometimes to look at what’s standing in the way of making different choices, and see what we can do to change it. Mary Beth Laughton is president and CEO of REI Co-op.

Industry News: William D. Nordhaus obituary: economist whose tools transformed climate policy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Nature)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Credit: Monica Jorge/Upcoming York Times/Redux/eyevine.
  • In a recent development, william (Bill) Nordhaus was an economist known for introducing climate change into economic analysis, earning him the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.
  • His research shaped our understanding of what drives economic growth and innovation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Credit: Monica Jorge/Upcoming York Times/Redux/eyevine.

In a recent development, william (Bill) Nordhaus was an economist known for introducing climate change into economic analysis, earning him the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Profoundly curious and able to distill complex issues to their core, Nordhaus produced groundbreaking scholarship powered by his joy of discovery, dedication to getting things right and commitment to ensuring that science serves society.

His research shaped our understanding of what drives economic growth and innovation. He realized that omitting the environment from economic measurement would send the wrong signals about the directions of economic growth and, therefore, pioneered more-inclusive ways to measure growth.

To build a better world, stop chasing economic growth.

To build a better world, stop chasing economic growth.

Nordhaus was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico. His father developed a ski area to the east of the city, and as a child, Nordhaus tried to derive models of snowfall. He earned an undergraduate degree in economics from Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1963, before moving to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, where he completed his PhD in 1967 under the supervision of future Nobel prizewinner Robert Solow. He then returned to Yale as an assistant professor and spent the rest of his academic career there.

Nordhaus rapidly made a name for himself by developing an early rigorous model for endogenous growth — that which occurs inside an economic system, rather than being driven by external factors. Before then, economic models had assumed that the rate of change in technology was independent of the economy.

It has been revealed that nordhaus’s PhD work showed that the pace of innovation depended on economic incentives, which could be altered by policy, such as through the patent system. His model also projected that research would face diminishing returns, with latest ideas getting harder to find — an idea that was validated 40 years later.

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality.

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality.

Industry observers note that next, he questioned the nature of economic growth. He recalled being inspired by an article in an in-flight magazine that described gross national product (GNP) as gross national pollution. In a 1972 article titled ‘Is Growth Obsolete?’, Nordhaus and economist James Tobin wrote that GNP exaggerates economic benefits by omitting environmental damage by “treating as free things which are not really free” and that “this practice gives the wrong signals for the directions of economic growth”. GNP also understates some of the benefits of economic growth, such as increased household well-being, from inventions such as electricity and home appliances.

This work alone gave rise to three influential lines of research: climate economics, the role of national accounts in measuring sustainable development and the importance of including new goods in measures of national income and economic well-being.

Nordhaus also considered the role of innovation. In a 1996 article on the history of the price of lighting, he measured the output and cost of various sources of light across human history (see go.nature.com/478rjyh). He showed that the light output per unit of energy of the compact fluorescent bulb was about 30,000 times greater than that of our distant ancestors’ fire.

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations.

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations.
